description: I’m building The Silent Signal Archivist, a free detective game that teaches school-age space fans why four NASA machines (Viking 1, Opportunity, the Apollo 11 seismometer and Voyager 1) went quiet, and what science they left behind. The game and pitch deck are already drafted, so you’d join a project with a clear plan. Looking for one teammate who enjoys storytelling, design or video, or helping test the game with students. Built for the “Abandoned but not Forgotten” challenge.
summary: Four NASA machines went quiet for four different reasons: a mistake, a storm, the heat, and a choice. The Silent Signal Archivist turns those stories into a free detective game for school-age space fans. Players investigate Viking 1, Opportunity, the Apollo 11 seismometer and Voyager 1. They run 3 of 4 diagnostic scans, read real evidence from NASA sources, and file a report on what ended each mission. Then they unlock the science each machine left behind. It answers the challenge by introducing students to NASA’s left-behind hardware and the discoveries it made possible, through a mystery they solve themselves. It matters because kids remember what they work out, and every silence teaches how real missions succeed and fail. It runs on any phone with no login, and every fact links to a NASA page.
details:
THE IDEA
What if a silent NASA machine was a case file? In The Silent Signal Archivist, students become junior archivists at a deep-space listening station. Four machines have gone quiet, and each silence has a different cause: a mistake (Viking 1), a storm (Opportunity), the heat (the Apollo 11 seismometer) and a choice (Voyager 1).

HOW IT WORKS
Each case opens with real NASA history and a dramatized signal log, labeled as fiction. Players get only 3 of 4 diagnostic scans, so they must choose carefully. Each scan reveals evidence from NASA sources, and some are red herrings. They then file a report on what ended the mission. Wasted scans and wrong reports cost stars (up to 3 per case, 12 in total). After solving, players see verified NASA facts with a source link, answer one check question, and read what the machine discovered plus a “Think about it” prompt. A final screen ranks them Junior, Senior or Maximum Archivist.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE
Instead of reading about the machines, students reason like mission engineers under limits. An interactive tau slider shows how a 2018 dust storm cut sunlight to Opportunity, labeled as a simplified model. Each case shows the real signal delay, and the closing question asks which silences engineers can prevent and which they can only prepare for.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
It is free, needs no login, and works on any phone. Every fact links to a NASA page, uncertain causes are labeled as NASA’s best explanation, and teacher notes are built in. It supports keyboard use, screen readers and reduced motion. We hope it makes NASA’s retired machines memorable for students and gives teachers a ready classroom activity.

TOOLS
HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript (canvas animations), hosted on Netlify, with the code public on GitHub: https://github.com/Zara-Khan15/silent-signal-archivist. We used an AI assistant (Claude) to help write the code and text, and Perplexity to cross-check facts, and we verified the facts against NASA pages.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
Accuracy first, with sources and honest labels. Accessibility. Kids’ attention, so each case takes only a few minutes. We built the first version before the event, and we spent the event fact-checking against NASA sources, preparing the deck, publishing the code and finishing this submission. Next steps are classroom playtests and more cases.
